pos: n. (reception with approval; the being received as true and worthy — rendering Greek apodoche)
etymology: Latin acceptatio, from acceptare, to take willingly. In the Authorized Version it never means bare acceptance of a fact; it means a saying received, welcomed, and rested upon.
biblical_def: Acceptation is the reception a true saying deserves and gets from a believing heart. Paul uses the word twice, and both times he stamps it upon a formula the churches already sang or recited: “This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (1Ti 1:15), and again, “This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation” (1Ti 4:9). The construction is doubled on purpose. The saying is faithful — it is true in itself, whether a man receives it or not. The saying is worthy of all acceptation — it lays an obligation on every man who hears it to receive it wholly, without reserve, without discount. Two things are therefore asserted at once: the objective truth of the gospel and the duty of every hearer toward it. The word all is not decoration. There is no partial acceptation of a faithful saying; a man who receives half of “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” has received none of it, for the half he keeps back is always the half that names him a sinner. Paul makes himself the pattern — “of whom I am chief” — so that no hearer may plead an exemption of degree.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives acceptation as acceptance; the state of being acceptable or favorably received; and, in its principal use, the received meaning of a word or expression.
webster_full: ACCEPTA'TION, n. Kind reception; a receiving with favor or approbation.
2. A state of being acceptable; favorable regard.
3. The meaning or sense in which a word or expression is understood, or generally received; as, a term is to be used in its usual acceptation.
4. Reception in general; the act of receiving that which is offered.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 1:15
This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.
1 Timothy 4:9
This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation.
1 Timothy 1:16
Howbeit for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might shew forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe on him to life everlasting.
Titus 3:8

This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men.
corruption_summary: The gospel is offered as an option to be considered rather than a faithful saying that is worthy of all acceptation and binds the conscience of every hearer.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern presentation of the gospel commonly stops at the first half of Paul's formula and drops the second. A message can be called true, well attested, historically credible, personally meaningful — and still be presented as one item on a shelf which the hearer may take or leave without guilt. That is not acceptation. Paul says the saying is worthy of all acceptation, which means the hearer who withholds it has not merely declined a preference; he has refused what he owed. Truth about Christ carries an obligation with it. The command to all men everywhere to repent (Act 17:30) is the same claim in another form.

The second corruption is the discount. Men will receive “Christ Jesus came into the world” gladly, and receive “to save sinners” on the understanding that the sinners are other people. Paul closes that door by putting himself at the head of the list — of whom I am chief — and then says in the next verse why: he was made a pattern, so that the worst case would be publicly settled and no later sinner could plead that his case was harder. An acceptation that admits the saying while denying its application to oneself has kept nothing.

A third, quieter loss is the loss of the faithful sayings themselves. The pastoral epistles show a young church with fixed, memorable, confessed formulas — sentences a congregation could hold in common and hand on. Where nothing is confessed in common, nothing can be received in common, and acceptation becomes a private opinion held privately. The confessions of the Reformed churches exist for exactly this reason: a faithful saying, written down, so that what is worthy of all acceptation may actually be accepted by all.
roots_summary: Greek apodoche (G594), acceptance, reception — used only of the faithful sayings in 1 Timothy; from apodechomai, to receive gladly.
roots_lines: Greek apodoche (G594) — acceptance, welcome reception; 1 Timothy 1:15 and 1 Timothy 4:9 only, both times of a faithful saying.
Greek apodechomai (G588) — to receive gladly, welcome; Acts 2:41 of those who gladly received the word.
Greek pistos ho logos — the “faithful saying” formula; five times in the pastoral epistles (1 Timothy 1:15, 3:1, 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8).
The doubling — faithful, and worthy of all acceptation — asserts the truth of the saying and the duty of the hearer in one breath.
Latin acceptatio, the taking of a thing offered; the English keeps the sense of a reception that approves what it receives.
usage: “A faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation” — true in itself, and binding on every hearer.
“Of whom I am chief” — Paul shuts the door on the discount before anyone reaches for it.
A saying received in part is not received; acceptation is of the whole or of nothing.

pos: v. (made like in form; shaped to a pattern — rendering Greek summorphos and suschematizo)
etymology: Latin conformare, to shape together, from con- (with) and forma (form). To be conformed is to take the shape of the mould one lies in.
biblical_def: Conformed appears at the two poles of the Christian life, and the two verses must be read together. The first is God's eternal purpose: “For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren” (Rom 8:29). The end for which the elect were chosen is not bare escape from wrath but a definite shape — the image of Christ, and Christ set forth as the elder brother of a great family all bearing His likeness. The second is the present command: “And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Rom 12:2). The same root, opposite direction. A man is always being shaped by something. The world presses continually toward its own form, and the pressure works on the outside — habits, speech, appetites, assumptions absorbed without argument. The remedy Paul names is not withdrawal but renewal, and it begins in the mind. Note carefully which conformity is passive and which is commanded. No man conforms himself to Christ's image; that is God's predestinating work, and it is certain. But the command not to be conformed to the world is addressed to the believer's will, and it must be obeyed daily. Sovereign purpose and present duty stand side by side in one epistle and neither weakens the other.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conform as to make like in form or manner; to bring into harmony or agreement with; and conformed as made to resemble, or brought to correspond with a pattern.
webster_full: CONFOR'MED, pp. Made to resemble; reduced to a likeness of.
CONFOR'M, v.t. To make like, in external appearance; to reduce to a like shape or form with something else.
2. To bring into harmony or correspondence; as, to conform our lives to the precepts of the gospel.
CONFOR'M, v.i. To comply with, or yield to; to live or act according to a rule or pattern.
scriptures: Romans 8:29
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
Romans 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
1 Peter 1:14
As obedient children, not fashioning yourselves according to the former lusts in your ignorance:
2 Corinthians 3:18
But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.
corruption_summary: Conformity to the world is reframed as cultural relevance, and the mind — the very place the renewal is commanded to begin — is treated as neutral ground.
corruption_paragraphs: The most successful conformity is the kind nobody notices, and the church has repeatedly adopted the world's form while believing itself to be merely translating the message. Paul locates the danger precisely: be not conformed to this world, and then, before any list of practices, he names the battlefield — the renewing of your mind. Conformity is not first a matter of what a Christian does but of what he assumes without examining: what counts as success, what makes a person valuable, what shame is for, what freedom means. These are absorbed by immersion, not by argument, which is why a man can hold orthodox doctrine and still be thoroughly conformed.

Romans 8:29 is also flattened when conformity to Christ's image is reduced to moral improvement. The verse says God predestinated it, so it will happen; and it says the goal is that Christ “might be the firstborn among many brethren,” so the goal is His glory in a family that resembles Him, not the individual's self-actualization. Second Corinthians 3:18 shows the means — beholding, and being changed from glory to glory by the Spirit. The believer is not told to sculpt himself; he is told where to look. What a man beholds, he comes to resemble, and that is as true of the world's images as of Christ's glory.
roots_summary: Greek summorphos (G4832), jointly formed, conformed to — Romans 8:29, Philippians 3:21; suschematizo (G4964), to fashion after a pattern — Romans 12:2, 1 Peter 1:14.
roots_lines: Greek summorphos (G4832) — jointly formed, similar in form; Romans 8:29 of the image of the Son, Philippians 3:21 of the body of His glory.
Greek suschematizo (G4964) — to conform to a scheme or outward fashion; Romans 12:2 and 1 Peter 1:14 only, both of the world's mould.
Greek metamorphoo (G3339) — to be transformed, the opposite motion in Romans 12:2; the same verb used of the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:2).
Greek anakainosis (G342) — renewing; Romans 12:2 and Titus 3:5, the Spirit's work in the mind.
The two Greek words differ: schema is the outward fashion that changes, morphe the settled form — the world gives a fashion, Christ gives a form.
usage: “Predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son” — the certain end of election.
“Be not conformed to this world” — the daily duty, addressed to the will.
“Changed into the same image” — a man comes to resemble what he beholds.

pos: v.t. (to lay hold of; to seize and hold fast — rendering Greek katalambano and piazo)
etymology: Latin apprehendere, to lay hold upon, from ad (to) and prehendere (to seize). The English later softened to mean understanding; the Authorized Version keeps the older, physical grip.
biblical_def: Apprehend in the Authorized Version means to seize and hold, not merely to comprehend. Paul takes the word into the greatest sentence he ever wrote about Christian effort: “Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus” (Php 3:12). Both hands are in the verse. Christ apprehended Paul on the Damascus road — seized him, arrested him, took him captive — and Paul spends the rest of his life reaching to lay hold of the thing for which he was laid hold of. The order is fixed and cannot be reversed: the apostle's pursuit is the answer to Christ's seizure, never its cause. The next verses show the posture of that pursuit: “I count not myself to have apprehended” (Php 3:13), and “I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Php 3:14). The word also keeps its plain legal use — the governor at Damascus was “desirous to apprehend” Paul (2Co 11:32), that is, to arrest him. The same verb serves the officer of a hostile king and the pursuing saint, and the double use is instructive: what men do to seize a prisoner, the believer does to seize Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apprehend as to take or seize; to take hold of with the hand; to arrest by legal process; and secondarily to conceive by the mind, to understand.
webster_full: APPREHEND', v.t. To take or seize; to take hold of.
2. To take with the hand or by legal process; to arrest; as, to apprehend a thief.
3. To take hold of with the understanding; to conceive in the mind; to understand, without passing a judgment or making an inference.
4. To fear; to entertain suspicion or fear of future evil.
scriptures: Philippians 3:12
Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus.
Philippians 3:13
Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before,
Philippians 3:14
I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
2 Corinthians 11:32
In Damascus the governor under Aretas the king kept the city of the Damascenes with a garrison, desirous to apprehend me:
corruption_summary: The word is reduced to mental comprehension, so that laying hold of Christ becomes understanding a doctrine about Him.
corruption_paragraphs: English drifted from grip to grasp, and the doctrine drifted with it. To apprehend Christ in Paul's sense is to seize and hold with the whole man; to apprehend Him in the modern sense is to have got the idea. A generation can be well catechized and never lay hold of anything. Philippians 3 forbids the substitution, because the same verb describes what Christ did to Paul on the road, and no one imagines Christ merely understood him there. Christ took him. The believer's answering act must be of the same order — a pursuit that costs, that presses, that counts nothing already attained.

The opposite corruption is equally common: a doctrine of effort with the first clause removed. Read alone, I follow after, if that I may apprehend could be made to teach a man climbing toward acceptance. Paul forecloses it in the same breath — that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus. He runs because he has been caught. The prize of the high calling is not wages earned by the running; it is the end of a course into which sovereign grace already placed him. Take away the first apprehending and the second becomes works; take away the second and the first becomes an excuse for sloth.
roots_summary: Greek katalambano (G2638), to seize eagerly, lay hold of — Philippians 3:12-13; piazo (G4084), to take, arrest — 2 Corinthians 11:32, John 7:30.
roots_lines: Greek katalambano (G2638) — to take eagerly, seize, possess; Philippians 3:12 twice, and of the darkness in John 1:5.
Greek piazo (G4084) — to seize, arrest, lay hands on; 2 Corinthians 11:32, John 7:30, Acts 12:4.
Latin apprehendere, to lay hold upon — the physical grip that the modern English sense has almost lost.
The same verb serves the arresting officer and the pursuing apostle; Scripture is not embarrassed by the violence of the image.
Philippians 3:12 sets the order permanently: Christ's seizure first, the believer's pursuit second and because of it.
usage: “That I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended” — the pursuit answers the seizure.
“I count not myself to have apprehended” — the mark of a man still running.
“Desirous to apprehend me” — the plain sense: to arrest.

pos: v. (archaic third person singular: warms, fosters, keeps tenderly — rendering Greek thalpo)
etymology: Old French cherir, to hold dear, from Latin carus, dear. The Greek behind it, thalpo, means literally to warm — the picture is a bird brooding over her young.
biblical_def: Cherisheth is the Authorized Version's word for warming and fostering what is one's own. It carries the whole weight of two commands. To husbands: “For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church” (Eph 5:29). To the pattern of ministry: “But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children” (1Th 2:7). The Greek word means to warm, and it is used of a bird covering her brood; the tenderness is not sentiment but the steady giving of one's own heat to something small and dependent. Paul's argument in Ephesians runs from the ordinary to the ultimate. Every man already knows how to nourish and cherish his own body without being commanded; that self-care is the measure God appoints for a husband toward his wife, and the pattern above both is Christ toward the church. Headship in Scripture is therefore never bare authority. It is authority that warms. The man who rules and does not cherish has not half-obeyed the command; he has broken it, for the standard is Christ, who gave Himself for the church (Eph 5:25). And the same word governs the minister: an apostle with authority to command chose instead to be gentle as a nursing mother among them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cherish as to treat with tenderness and affection; to give warmth, ease or comfort to; to nurse, support and nurture.
webster_full: CHER'ISH, v.t. To treat with tenderness and affection; to give warmth, ease or comfort to.
2. To hold as dear; to embrace with affection; to foster and encourage; as, to cherish the principles of virtue.
3. To nurse, to nurture, to support; as, to cherish an infant.
CHER'ISHETH, the third person singular of cherish, in the older English of the Authorized Version.
scriptures: Ephesians 5:29
For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church:
1 Thessalonians 2:7
But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children:
Ephesians 5:25
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
Ephesians 5:28
So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies. He that loveth his wife loveth himself.
corruption_summary: Headship is preached without cherishing, and the answer offered to that failure is the abolition of headship rather than its recovery.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors stand opposite each other and both destroy the text. The first is the household where a man claims the authority of Ephesians 5 and never reads to the end of the sentence. Scripture gives him no such office. The command is to love as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it, and to nourish and cherish as a man does his own body — a standard measured in self-expenditure, not in compliance extracted. A husband who is obeyed and does not cherish is not a strong head; he is a disobedient one, and the wife's submission does not repair his sin.

The second error offers to fix the first by removing the order altogether, as though headship itself were the injury. But the abuse of an office is not an argument against the office. Paul grounds the whole passage in Christ and the church, and that ground cannot be moved without moving the gospel it pictures. Erase the order and you have not liberated the wife; you have destroyed the image by which the Lord chose to display His love for His people. What Ephesians 5 requires is not less headship but headship that warms, and 1 Thessalonians 2:7 shows the same shape in the church: an apostle with every right to command, gentle among them as a nurse cherisheth her children.
roots_summary: Greek thalpo (G2282), to warm, to brood over, hence to foster — Ephesians 5:29 and 1 Thessalonians 2:7 only; Hebrew chabab (H2245), to cherish with affection.
roots_lines: Greek thalpo (G2282) — to warm, brood, cherish; Ephesians 5:29 and 1 Thessalonians 2:7, its only two occurrences.
Greek ektrepho (G1625) — to nourish, rear to maturity; the companion verb in Ephesians 5:29 and 6:4.
Hebrew chabab (H2245) — to hide in the bosom, to cherish with affection; Deuteronomy 33:3.
The image is a bird covering her young: warmth given from the one who has it to the one who has none.
The Old French cherir and Latin carus supply the English sense of holding dear; the Greek supplies the sense of keeping warm.
usage: “Nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church” — the measure of headship.
“Even as a nurse cherisheth her children” — apostolic authority, gently used.
A husband obeyed but not cherishing has broken the command, not half-kept it.

pos: n. pl. (those who believe; the ordinary New Testament name for the members of the church)
etymology: From Old English gelyfan, to believe, to hold dear. The plural noun renders the Greek participle hoi pisteuontes, “the believing ones,” and the adjective pistos used substantively.
biblical_def: Believers is one of the plainest names Scripture gives the church, and it is a name of the whole company, not of an inner circle. Luke records the growth of the Jerusalem church in exactly this word: “And believers were the more added to the Lord, multitudes both of men and women” (Act 5:14). Two things are asserted there. First, they were added to the Lord — the joining is to a Person before it is to a society. Second, they were believers, which is to say the mark of membership was faith, not birth, not nationality, not ceremony. Paul charges Timothy to “be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity” (1Ti 4:12), and the six terms show what a believer's life is expected to look like from the outside. The same company appears in its common life: “the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul” (Act 4:32), and “all that believed were together, and had all things common” (Act 2:44). Believers in the New Testament are never solitary. The word is plural because faith gathers, and the gathering is visible: a body of men and women, known to each other, added to the Lord and therefore added to one another.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a believer as one who believes; one who gives credit to other evidence than that of personal knowledge; and in theology, one who gives credit to the truth of the Scriptures as a revelation from God.
webster_full: BELIEV'ER, n. One who believes; one who gives credit to other evidence than that of personal knowledge.
2. In theology, one who gives credit to the truth of the Scriptures, as a revelation from God.
3. In a more restricted sense, a professor of Christianity; one who receives the gospel, as unfolding the true way of salvation, and Christ as his Savior.
BELIEV'ERS, the plural; in the Scriptures, the whole company of those added to the Lord.
scriptures: Acts 5:14
And believers were the more added to the Lord, multitudes both of men and women.
1 Timothy 4:12
Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
Acts 4:32
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
Acts 2:44
And all that believed were together, and had all things common;
corruption_summary: Belief is privatized, so that a believer is understood as an individual holding an opinion rather than a member added to the Lord and to a visible body.
corruption_paragraphs: The New Testament has no category for a believer who belongs to no congregation. Luke does not say that believers increased and then, separately, that a church formed; he says believers were added to the Lord, and the immediate consequence in Acts is a body of one heart and one soul with its goods held loosely. The modern habit of treating faith as a private conviction, with church attendance as an optional expression of it, reverses the order of the text. Faith in Christ joins a man to Christ, and no one is joined to the Head without being joined to the members.

The second loss is the visibility of the mark. Paul tells Timothy to be an example of the believers in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity — six things others can observe. A believer in Scripture is identifiable: he confesses, he gathers, he gives, he lives differently. Where belief becomes an inward disposition with no required outward shape, the word ceases to name anything, and a church roll fills with names that Acts would not have counted. This is not a plea for perfectionism; it is the plain expectation that what a man believes will show.
roots_summary: Greek pisteuo (G4100), to believe, trust; its participle hoi pisteuontes, the believing ones; pistos (G4103), faithful, believing, used as a noun for the church's members.
roots_lines: Greek pisteuo (G4100) — to believe, entrust oneself to; over two hundred and forty times in the New Testament.
Greek pistos (G4103) — faithful, believing; used substantively of church members in 1 Timothy 4:12 and Acts 10:45.
Greek pistis (G4102) — faith, the thing believed and the believing; Hebrews 11:1.
Acts 5:14 says believers were added to the Lord — the union is with Christ first, and with the body because of Him.
The plural is the New Testament's ordinary form; the singular believer standing alone is nearly unknown in Acts.
usage: “Believers were the more added to the Lord” — added to Him, and so to one another.
“Be thou an example of the believers” — in six things others can see.
“All that believed were together” — Acts knows no solitary Christian.

pos: v. (archaic: was necessary for, was fitting and required — rendering Greek dei)
etymology: Old English behofian, to have need of, to be needful. In the Authorized Version it carries the force of a divine necessity, not a mere propriety.
biblical_def: Behoved is the Authorized Version's word for what must be, and the New Testament uses it of the sufferings of Christ. On the Emmaus road and again in the upper room the risen Lord opens the Scriptures with it: “Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day” (Luk 24:46). The necessity is not physical but covenantal. Nothing compelled the Son of God from outside; the must arises from the eternal counsel of God and from the written word which that counsel had already given. Hence the Lord's earlier question in the same chapter: “Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?” (Luk 24:26). Hebrews applies the same word to the incarnation itself: “Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people” (Heb 2:17). The logic is exact. If He is to be a priest for men, He must be made like the men He represents; if He is to make reconciliation, He must have something to offer, and He must be able to die. The likeness was real and entire, sin excepted — He took part of the same flesh and blood (Heb 2:14), and by death destroyed him that had the power of death.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines behove as to be necessary for; to be fit or meet for; to be proper, or requisite in the circumstances of the case.
webster_full: BEHOOVE, BEHOVE, v.t. To be necessary for; to be fit for; to be meet for, with respect to necessity, duty or convenience.
2. It is used chiefly impersonally: it behoveth, it behoved — that is, it is or was required by necessity or fitness.
3. In the Scriptures the word carries the force of a necessity arising from the purpose and promise of God, as, thus it behoved Christ to suffer.
BEHO'VED, pp. Was necessary or requisite for.
scriptures: Luke 24:46
And said unto them, Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day:
Hebrews 2:17

Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people.
Luke 24:26
Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?
Hebrews 2:14

Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;
corruption_summary: The necessity of the cross is denied outright, as though God might have forgiven without atonement, or reduced to tragic accident rather than eternal purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: The claim that God could simply have pardoned sin without the cross, and that the crucifixion was therefore an avoidable cruelty, runs directly against the Lord's own exposition. He did not say it was one way among several; He said it behoved Christ to suffer, and He said so out of the Scriptures. The necessity is grounded in God's own justice, which cannot clear the guilty without satisfaction, and in God's own promise, which had been written down beforehand. To call the atonement unnecessary is to make God's justice negotiable and His word provisional.

The opposite corruption empties the word of purpose and makes Calvary a miscarriage of Roman and Jewish justice that God afterward turned to good account. Peter's sermon closes that reading in a single sentence: Christ was delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and by wicked hands crucified and slain (Act 2:23). Both halves stand. The men who did it are guilty; the doing of it was decreed. Behoved is the word that holds the second half in place.

Hebrews 2:17 guards the incarnation against the same erosion. It behoved Him to be made like unto His brethren — not to appear so, not partially so, but really so, that He might be a merciful and faithful high priest. Every scheme that thins out the true humanity of Christ, ancient or modern, cuts the nerve of the priesthood, for a priest who is not of the people cannot represent them, and a body that cannot die cannot be offered.
roots_summary: Greek dei (G1163), it is necessary, must needs — the impersonal verb of divine necessity, used of Christ's suffering, and opheilo (G3784), to owe, be bound, in Hebrews 2:17.
roots_lines: Greek dei (G1163) — it is necessary, it behoved; Luke 24:46, Luke 9:22, John 3:14, Acts 1:16.
Greek opheilo (G3784) — to owe, to be under obligation; Hebrews 2:17, where the necessity is that of the office He undertook.
Old English behofian, to have need of; the archaic English preserves an impersonal construction the modern tongue has lost.
The necessity is never external compulsion upon God, but the fitness required by His own justice and the certainty of His own promise.
Luke 24:26 puts the same necessity as a question — Ought not Christ to have suffered? — and expects the answer from the Scriptures.
usage: “Thus it behoved Christ to suffer” — opened out of the written word, not out of circumstance.
“In all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren” — the priesthood requires the incarnation.
The must of the cross is God's justice and God's promise, never man's compulsion.

pos: adj. (crushed in heart; shattered inwardly — rendering Hebrew shabar leb and Greek suntribo ten kardian)
etymology: A compound of broken and heart. The Hebrew and Greek behind it both mean literally shattered, as a vessel is shattered — not merely saddened.
biblical_def: Brokenhearted names those the Messiah was anointed to reach. Isaiah's commission reads: “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Isa 61:1). The Lord Jesus stood in the synagogue at Nazareth and read that scripture over Himself: “he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted” (Luk 4:18). The word is strong. It does not mean disappointed; it means shattered, as pottery is shattered, and it describes a man whose inward frame has given way under sin, loss, or the weight of God's hand. Scripture treats such men with a tenderness it shows to no other class: “The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit” (Psa 34:18); “He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds” (Psa 147:3). There is a further and crucial sense. In the Psalms a broken heart is not only the wound God heals but the offering God accepts: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. Brokenness is therefore both the misery Christ came to bind up and the only condition in which a sinner ever comes to Him at all. God does not despise it; He draws near to it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines brokenhearted as having the spirits depressed or crushed by grief or despair; and notes its scriptural use of one whose heart is subdued and contrite before God.
webster_full: BROKEN-HEART'ED, a. Having the spirits depressed or crushed by grief or despair.
2. In the Scriptures, having the heart subdued, humbled and contrite; as, the Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart.
BRO'KEN, pp. Parted by violence; rent asunder; infirm; made bankrupt.
HEART, n. The seat of the affections, the will and the understanding; in Scripture, the whole inner man.
scriptures: Isaiah 61:1

The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;
Luke 4:18

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,
Psalm 34:18
The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
Psalm 51:17
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
corruption_summary: Brokenness is treated as a psychological condition to be managed and relieved, and the brokenness God requires before Himself is quietly dropped as unhealthy.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture keeps two things together which the therapeutic register cannot hold at once: God binds up the brokenhearted, and God requires a broken heart. Psalm 51 calls it the sacrifice God will not despise; Psalm 34 says He is near to it. When brokenness is redefined as damage — a state to be repaired so that a person may return to functioning — the second half becomes unintelligible, and men are counselled out of the very posture in which God meets them. The gospel does not offer to restore a man's self-regard. It offers a Physician to those who know they are shattered.

The opposite failure is to preach brokenness without the binding up. Isaiah 61:1 and Luke 4:18 are commissions of mercy: to bind up, to heal, to proclaim liberty, to open the prison. A ministry that leaves men crushed and calls the crushing itself sanctification has stopped where Christ began. The anointing is for healing, and the healing is real. What Scripture refuses is the shortcut — comfort administered to a man who has not yet come to the end of himself, which soothes the symptom and leaves him unhealed.
roots_summary: Hebrew shabar (H7665), to break, shatter, with leb (H3820), heart; Greek suntribo (G4937), to crush completely, with kardia (G2588), heart.
roots_lines: Hebrew shabar (H7665) — to break in pieces, shatter; used of vessels, of bones, and of the heart in Psalm 51:17 and Isaiah 61:1.
Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart; in Scripture the whole inner man, mind, will and affections together.
Hebrew dakka (H1793) — contrite, crushed; the companion word in Psalm 34:18 and Isaiah 57:15.
Greek suntribo (G4937) — to crush completely, shatter; Luke 4:18 of the brokenhearted, Romans 16:20 of Satan bruised.
Greek kardia (G2588) — the heart, the seat of thought and will, not merely of feeling.
usage: “He hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted” — read by the Lord over Himself at Nazareth.
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart” — nearness, not distance, is God's answer.
“A broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” — the one sacrifice a sinner can bring.

pos: n. (a carrying forward; advancement, progress — rendering Greek prokope)
etymology: From further, Old English furthra, to advance. The Greek prokope was a military and pioneering word: the cutting forward of a way where none existed.
biblical_def: Furtherance is the Authorized Version's word for the gospel's advance, and Paul uses it from a prison. “But I would ye should understand, brethren, that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel” (Php 1:12). The Philippians had assumed the apostle's chains were a setback; Paul tells them the chains were the road. The Greek word pictures pioneers cutting a way forward through obstacles, and that is exactly Paul's claim — the imprisonment did not slow the gospel down, it opened ground the gospel could not otherwise have reached, into the palace guard and beyond. He uses the word again of the church itself: “I know that I shall abide and continue with you all for your furtherance and joy of faith” (Php 1:25). There is a furtherance of the gospel in the world and a furtherance of faith in the saints, and Paul's life is spent on both. Beneath the word lies a doctrine of providence with no soft edges. The advance is God's work, not the apostle's management of circumstances: “he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Php 1:6), and “I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). Men may be bound; the word never is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines furtherance as a helping forward; promotion; advancement; the act of carrying a thing onward toward its end.
webster_full: FUR'THERANCE, n. A helping forward; promotion; advancement.
FUR'THER, v.t. To help forward; to promote; to advance; to forward; to help or assist.
2. To countenance; to support; to patronize.
FUR'THERER, n. One who helps to advance; a promoter.
scriptures: Philippians 1:12
But I would ye should understand, brethren, that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel;
Philippians 1:25
And having this confidence, I know that I shall abide and continue with you all for your furtherance and joy of faith;
Philippians 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
2 Timothy 2:9
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
corruption_summary: Advance is measured by visible success, so that the very providences God uses to further the gospel are read as its defeat.
corruption_paragraphs: The church is perpetually tempted to reckon the gospel's progress by numbers, favour, and freedom of operation, and by that reckoning Paul's imprisonment was a catastrophe. He says the opposite: the things which happened unto him fell out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel. This is not a brave face put on a bad situation. It is a judgment about how God actually advances His word — often through constraint, loss, and the closing of the doors men would have chosen. A ministry that treats every hindrance as an attack to be escaped will keep trying to open the door God shut in order to open another.

The second corruption is the reverse — a fatalism that stops working because God will do it anyway. Philippians will not permit that either. Paul expects to abide and continue with them for their furtherance and joy of faith; his continued labour is the means by which their progress comes. God's certainty of finishing the good work He began is the ground of effort, not its substitute. The word of God is not bound, and therefore the man in bonds keeps preaching.
roots_summary: Greek prokope (G4297), a cutting forward, advancement — Philippians 1:12, 1:25, 1 Timothy 4:15; from prokopto, to cut a way forward.
roots_lines: Greek prokope (G4297) — progress, advancement; Philippians 1:12 and 1:25, and 1 Timothy 4:15 of Timothy's own profiting.
Greek prokopto (G4298) — to cut forward, blaze a trail; Luke 2:52, Galatians 1:14, 2 Timothy 3:13.
The image is of pioneers clearing a way through forest or enemy ground — advance made through obstacles, not around them.
Philippians 1:12 makes providence the pioneer: the chains themselves cut the road into the palace guard.
2 Timothy 2:9 gives the limit of every persecution — the preacher is bound, the word is not.
usage: “Fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel” — the chains were the road.
“Your furtherance and joy of faith” — the saints advance as well as the gospel.
“The word of God is not bound” — the prison holds the man only.

pos: adv. (kindly, humanely, with friendly consideration — rendering Greek philanthropos and philophronos)
etymology: From courteous, the manner proper to a court, Old French corteis. The Greek words behind it are stronger than mere politeness: one means humanely, love toward man; the other, with friendliness of mind.
biblical_def: Courteously occurs twice in the Authorized Version, both times in the closing chapters of Acts, and both times toward a prisoner. “And the next day we touched at Sidon. And Julius courteously entreated Paul, and gave him liberty to go unto his friends to refresh himself” (Act 27:3). Julius was a Roman centurion with a chained apostle in his charge and no obligation to show him anything; the Greek word Luke uses means humanely, out of love toward man. Later, shipwrecked on Melita, “the chief man of the island, whose name was Publius; who received us, and lodged us three days courteously” (Act 28:7). Both men were pagans, and Scripture records their kindness without embarrassment, as a real good done to God's servant. The virtue is commanded of Christians in plainer words: “Finally, be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous” (1Pe 3:8), and “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt” (Col 4:6). Courtesy in Scripture is not a social lubricant or a substitute for truth; it is the ordinary form love takes in the presence of a stranger, an inferior, or an enemy. Peter sets it in a list of hard graces — unity, compassion, brotherly love, pity — and it belongs there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines courteously as in a courteous manner; with obliging civility and complaisance; kindly.
webster_full: COUR'TEOUSLY, adv. In a courteous manner; with civility, kindness and complaisance.
COUR'TEOUS, a. Polite; well bred; being of elegant manners; civil; obliging; condescending.
2. In the Scriptures, kind and humane toward strangers and inferiors; as, Julius courteously entreated Paul.
COUR'TESY, n. Elegance or politeness of manners; civility; complaisance; an act of kindness or civility.
scriptures: Acts 27:3
And the next day we touched at Sidon. And Julius courteously entreated Paul, and gave him liberty to go unto his friends to refresh himself.
Acts 28:7
In the same quarters were possessions of the chief man of the island, whose name was Publius; who received us, and lodged us three days courteously.
1 Peter 3:8
Finally, be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous:
Colossians 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
corruption_summary: Courtesy is set against conviction, so that a man is told he must choose between being kind and being clear.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors divide the field, and Scripture rejects both. The first treats courtesy as the whole duty — a manner so anxious to give no offence that it will not say what is true, and calls its silence love. Colossians 4:6 will not allow it: speech is to be with grace and seasoned with salt, and salt is not a softening agent. The second treats courtesy as weakness, and mistakes rudeness for fidelity. Peter lists it with compassion, brotherly love and pity as a mark of those who will inherit a blessing, and he says so in a passage about suffering for righteousness. A man who cannot be kind under provocation has not become bold; he has become coarse.

The two occurrences in Acts add something a professing church needs to hear. Both the centurion and the chief man of Melita were pagans, and Luke records their kindness plainly as kindness. Common decency in unbelievers is real, and Christians who cannot acknowledge it discredit their own message. It does not save the men who show it — Cornelius, devout as he was, still needed to send for Peter — but it is a genuine good, restrained by God's common grace, and it shames a believer who gives less.
roots_summary: Greek philanthropos (G5364), humanely, out of love toward man — Acts 27:3; philophronos (G5390), with friendliness of mind — Acts 28:7; philophron (G5391), courteous — 1 Peter 3:8.
roots_lines: Greek philanthropos (G5364) — humanely, kindly toward men; Acts 27:3 only, of the centurion Julius.
Greek philophronos (G5390) — with friendliness of mind; Acts 28:7 only, of Publius on Melita.
Greek philanthropia (G5363) — love toward man; Titus 3:4, of the kindness of God our Saviour appearing.
The root phil- makes courtesy a species of love, not a species of manners.
Colossians 4:6 gives the balance: grace in the speech, salt in the substance.
usage: “Julius courteously entreated Paul” — a Roman officer to a chained prisoner.
“Lodged us three days courteously” — heathen kindness recorded as real kindness.
“Speech alway with grace, seasoned with salt” — both, never one without the other.

pos: adj. (dwelling among; having habitual intercourse with — rendering Hebrew halak, to walk)
etymology: Latin conversari, to turn oneself about among, to keep company with. The older English kept the sense of living among; the modern sense of being well informed is a late thinning of the word.
biblical_def: Conversant in the Authorized Version means dwelling among, keeping daily company with, and it stands behind the older English word conversation, which meant a manner of life and not talk. Joshua reads the law before the whole congregation, “with the women, and the little ones, and the strangers that were conversant among them” (Jos 8:35) — the strangers who lived among Israel, whose lives were bound up with hers. David's men are described by Nabal's servant: “the men were very good unto us, and we were not hurt, neither missed we any thing, as long as we were conversant with them, when we were in the fields” (1Sa 25:15). The Hebrew is the ordinary verb to walk; being conversant with a man is walking with him, and the test of what a man is comes out in that walking. This is exactly why the New Testament uses conversation for the whole visible life: “Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ” (Php 1:27), and “as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation” (1Pe 1:15). A man's doctrine is heard; his conversation is watched. Nabal's shepherds did not report David's creed; they reported that nothing went missing in the fields.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conversant as keeping company; having frequent or customary intercourse; living among or with; and secondarily, acquainted by familiar use or study.
webster_full: CON'VERSANT, a. Keeping company; having frequent or customary intercourse; intimately associating; familiar by fellowship.
2. Acquainted by familiar use or study; as, a man conversant with the Scriptures.
3. Concerning; having concern or relation to; as, education is conversant about the young.
CONVERSA'TION, n. General course of manners; behavior; deportment; especially as it respects morals.
scriptures: Joshua 8:35
There was not a word of all that Moses commanded, which Joshua read not before all the congregation of Israel, with the women, and the little ones, and the strangers that were conversant among them.
1 Samuel 25:15
But the men were very good unto us, and we were not hurt, neither missed we any thing, as long as we were conversant with them, when we were in the fields:
Philippians 1:27

Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;
1 Peter 1:15
But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation;
corruption_summary: The word has thinned from a life lived among men to information possessed about a subject, and the same thinning has happened to Christian profession.
corruption_paragraphs: To be conversant once meant to dwell with; it now means to be informed about. A man may be perfectly conversant with the doctrine of sanctification in the modern sense and utterly unsanctified in the older one. The drift is not merely lexical. Where Christianity is understood as a body of information to be mastered, church life becomes the transfer of content and the visible walk drops out of the test entirely. Scripture measures otherwise. Nabal's servant vouched for David's men on the evidence of months in the fields: nothing hurt, nothing missing.

Joshua 8:35 carries a second charge worth naming. The whole law was read before the women, the little ones, and the strangers conversant among them — nobody was reckoned incapable of hearing the word of God, and nobody was excused from it. Where a congregation is sorted into audiences and the strangers among it are given something lighter than the Scriptures, that assembly has not become welcoming; it has withheld from its hearers the only thing it was given to hand them.
roots_summary: Hebrew halak (H1980), to walk, go, live among; the Authorized Version renders it conversant where the walking is a settled dwelling with others. Greek anastrophe (G391), manner of life, lies behind the New Testament conversation.
roots_lines: Hebrew halak (H1980) — to walk, go, behave; Joshua 8:35 and 1 Samuel 25:15 of dwelling among.
Greek anastrophe (G391) — manner of life, conduct; 1 Peter 1:15, Galatians 1:13, Ephesians 4:22.
Greek politeuomai (G4176) — to live as a citizen; Philippians 1:27, where the conversation is to become the gospel.
Latin conversari, to turn about among — the old English kept the dwelling, the modern kept only the knowing.
Wherever the Authorized Version says conversation it means the whole visible life, never speech alone.
usage: “The strangers that were conversant among them” — and the whole law was read in their hearing.
“As long as we were conversant with them” — character proved by months in the fields.
“Holy in all manner of conversation” — the walk, not the talk.

pos: v.t. (to search out, test, try — rendering Greek anakrino, dokimazo, and Hebrew bachan)
etymology: Latin examinare, to weigh, from examen, the tongue of a balance. To examine is to put a thing in the scales and see what it weighs.
biblical_def: Examine in Scripture is a work a man does upon himself, a work God does upon a man, and a work a church does at the Table. The command at the Supper is explicit: “But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup” (1Co 11:28). Paul addresses the whole Corinthian church with a wider and sharper form: “Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves” (2Co 13:5). The question is not whether a man feels at peace but whether he is in the faith at all, and the test is applied by the man to himself, in the presence of God. David asks God to do the searching, since a man cannot see his own bottom: “Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart” (Psa 26:2). And Paul submits his ministry to examination by others without resentment: “Mine answer to them that do examine me is this” (1Co 9:3). The Latin behind the English is a balance-beam, and the picture is exact. Examination is weighing — laying a life beside a fixed standard and reading the result honestly. The standard is never the man himself, his sincerity, or his comparison with other men; it is the word of God and the Christ it reveals.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines examine as to inspect carefully with a view to discover truth; to search or inquire into facts; to try by a rule or law; to interrogate.
webster_full: EXAM'INE, v.t. To inspect carefully, with a view to discover truth or the real state of a thing.
2. To search or inquire into facts and circumstances by interrogating; as, to examine a witness.
3. To look into the state of a subject; to view in all its aspects; to weigh arguments and compare facts.
4. To try by a rule or law; as, to examine ourselves by the standard of the word of God.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 11:28
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
2 Corinthians 13:5
Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.
Psalm 26:2
Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart.
1 Corinthians 9:3
Mine answer to them that do examine me is this,
corruption_summary: Self-examination is dismissed as morbid introspection, and assurance is grounded in a remembered decision that no one is permitted to test.
corruption_paragraphs: An entire style of teaching now treats 2 Corinthians 13:5 as dangerous — as though asking whether one is in the faith must undermine assurance. Paul commands it of a whole congregation. The command exists because a man can be deceived about himself, and because the deception is comfortable and will not lift on its own. True assurance is not damaged by examination; it is confirmed by it, since the same apostle expects most of them to find Christ in them. What examination destroys is false assurance, and the destruction of a false assurance is a mercy, however it feels at the time.

The opposite corruption is examination without an object: a man turning inward and searching his own feelings for evidence, which is introspection, not obedience. Scripture never sends a man to look for warmth in himself. The test in 2 Corinthians is whether ye be in the faith, and the faith has content and a Christ; the test at the Table is whether a man discerns the Lord's body. David's prayer shows the safe posture — he asks God to do the trying, and then walks in integrity. Self-examination that never lifts its eyes to Christ ends in either despair or self-flattery, and both are false readings of the scale.
roots_summary: Greek anakrino (G350), to scrutinize, investigate judicially; dokimazo (G1381), to test and approve; Hebrew bachan (H974), to test as metals are tested.
roots_lines: Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, scrutinize; 1 Corinthians 9:3, 1 Corinthians 2:15, Acts 17:11 of the Bereans searching the Scriptures.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test with a view to approving; 1 Corinthians 11:28, Romans 12:2, 1 Thessalonians 5:21.
Greek peirazo (G3985) — to test, try, or tempt; 2 Corinthians 13:5, where the church is told to test itself.
Hebrew bachan (H974) — to assay metal, to prove; Psalm 26:2, Jeremiah 17:10, Zechariah 13:9.
The Latin examen is the tongue of a balance — examination is weighing against a standard outside the self.
usage: “Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat” — the Table requires it, and does not bar him from it.
“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith” — commanded to a whole church.
“Examine me, O LORD” — David asks for the searching he cannot perform on himself.

pos: v. (to do habitually; to carry out repeatedly — rendering Greek prasso and Hebrew paal)
etymology: Greek praktike, from prassein, to do. The Authorized Version spells the verb with an s after the older English pattern; the noun is practice.
biblical_def: Practise in the Authorized Version is a heavy word, and it is almost always used of evil. The Psalmist prays to be kept from it: “Incline not my heart to any evil thing, to practise wicked works with men that work iniquity: and let me not eat of their dainties” (Psa 141:4). Micah describes men who lie awake devising: “Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it, because it is in the power of their hand” (Mic 2:1). Isaiah names the vile person who works iniquity “to practise hypocrisy, and to utter error against the LORD” (Isa 32:6). Daniel foretells a king who “shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper, and practise, and shall destroy the mighty and the holy people” (Dan 8:24). The word therefore names sin at a particular stage: not the sudden fall but the settled habit, planned in the night and executed in the morning because the hand has power to do it. This is why the Psalmist prays about his heart rather than his circumstances. Practice begins with an inclination, becomes a device, and ends as a trade. Micah adds the reason such men do it — because it is in the power of their hand — which is to say, ability was mistaken for permission.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines practise as to do or perform frequently, customarily or habitually; to exercise any profession; and notes the habitual sense which distinguishes it from a single act.
webster_full: PRAC'TISE, v.t. To do or perform frequently, customarily or habitually; to perform by a succession of acts; as, to practise gaming.
2. To exercise any profession or art; as, to practise law or medicine.
3. To use or exercise; as, to practise deceit.
PRAC'TISE, v.i. To use or exercise any profession or art; also, to form a habit of acting in any manner.
scriptures: Psalm 141:4
Incline not my heart to any evil thing, to practise wicked works with men that work iniquity: and let me not eat of their dainties.
Micah 2:1
Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it, because it is in the power of their hand.
Isaiah 32:6

For the vile person will speak villany, and his heart will work iniquity, to practise hypocrisy, and to utter error against the LORD, to make empty the soul of the hungry, and he will cause the drink of the thirsty to fail.
Daniel 8:24
And his power shall be mighty, but not by his own power: and he shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper, and practise, and shall destroy the mighty and the holy people.
corruption_summary: Ability is treated as permission — what is in the power of the hand is assumed to be lawful for the hand to do.
corruption_paragraphs: Micah gives the reasoning of the wicked in five words: because it is in the power of their hand. That is the whole argument, and it has not changed. Whatever a man, a corporation, or a state acquires the capacity to do, it comes to regard as permitted, and the question of lawfulness is settled by the question of capability. Scripture calls this the practice of iniquity and pronounces woe upon it. The rule of God's law over what men are able to do is precisely what the word denies, and every generation that gains a new power must be told again that ability confers no right.

The second thing Micah exposes is the planning. These men devise upon their beds and execute in the morning light; the sin is not a stumble but a project. Psalm 141:4 therefore prays at the right point — not keep my hands from wicked works but incline not my heart — and adds a request that sounds strange until one has seen it happen: let me not eat of their dainties. Practised sin recruits by hospitality. A man is first at the table, then in the plan, then in the deed. Isaiah 32:6 names the same progression in another key, where practised hypocrisy ends by emptying the soul of the hungry — settled sin always finally lands on the weak.
roots_summary: Greek prasso (G4238), to do repeatedly or habitually; Hebrew paal (H6466), to do or make systematically; alal (H5953), to effect thoroughly, in a bad sense to practise.
roots_lines: Greek prasso (G4238) — to practise, perform habitually; John 3:20, Romans 1:32, Romans 2:1-3.
Hebrew paal (H6466) — to do or make systematically and habitually; Psalm 141:4, Micah 2:1.
Hebrew alal (H5953) — to effect thoroughly; used in a bad sense of practising evil, Psalm 141:4.
Hebrew kashaph (H3784) — to practise sorcery; the word behind the prohibition of the witch in Exodus 22:18.
The Greek distinguishes prasso, the habitual doing, from poieo, the single act — practice is sin become a trade.
usage: “Incline not my heart… to practise wicked works” — the prayer goes to the heart, not the hands.
“Because it is in the power of their hand” — ability mistaken for permission.
“Let me not eat of their dainties” — practised sin recruits at the table first.

pos: v. (to be enough; to satisfy fully — rendering Greek arkeo and Hebrew rab)
etymology: Latin sufficere, to supply, to be adequate, from sub and facere. The Authorized Version uses it both of provision that is enough and of sin that has gone on long enough.
biblical_def: Suffice in the Authorized Version has two distinct uses, and both are worth marking. The first is provision. When Moses doubted that God could feed six hundred thousand men, he asked, “Shall the flocks and the herds be slain for them, to suffice them? or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together for them, to suffice them?” (Num 11:22) — a question the LORD answered by asking whether His hand was waxed short. The second use is far sharper: it is God calling time on sin. To Moses, who kept asking to enter the land: “the LORD said unto me, Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter” (Deu 3:26). To the princes of Israel: “Let it suffice you, O princes of Israel: remove violence and spoil, and execute judgment and justice” (Eze 45:9). And Peter to the churches: “For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries” (1Pe 4:3). Peter's use is the sternest kindness in the epistle. Enough of that life has been lived already; not one hour more is owed to it. The word does not say the past was tolerable, but that it is finished, and that a man who has spent years in it has no arrears to pay to his old master.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines suffice as to be enough or sufficient; to be equal to the end proposed; and transitively, to satisfy, to content, to be equal to the wants of.
webster_full: SUFFI'CE, v.i. To be enough; to be sufficient; to be equal to the end proposed.
2. To satisfy; to content; as, let it suffice thee.
SUFFI'CE, v.t. To satisfy; to afford or supply what is desired; as, the meat sufficed the multitude.
SUFFI'CIENT, a. Enough; equal to the end proposed; adequate to wants.
scriptures: 1 Peter 4:3
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
Deuteronomy 3:26
But the LORD was wroth with me for your sakes, and would not hear me: and the LORD said unto me, Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter.
Ezekiel 45:9
Thus saith the Lord GOD; Let it suffice you, O princes of Israel: remove violence and spoil, and execute judgment and justice, take away your exactions from my people, saith the Lord GOD.
Numbers 11:22
Shall the flocks and the herds be slain for them, to suffice them? or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together for them, to suffice them?
corruption_summary: A man tells himself he has time yet for the old life, and treats his past bondage as an unpaid claim upon his present.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter's sentence is aimed at a particular self-deception: the notion that a converted man is owed some remainder of his former pleasures, that having given up so much he may keep a little. The time past of our life may suffice settles the account. The years already spent were more than enough; the old master has been paid in full and has no further claim. Where this is not believed, sanctification becomes a slow negotiation in which the flesh is granted terms, and terms granted to the flesh are never final.

Deuteronomy 3:26 shows the other edge, and it falls on a servant of God, not on a rebel. Moses asked repeatedly to cross over, and the LORD said, Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter. God's refusals are not always reversed by persistence, and a settled no from Him is mercy, not deafness — Moses saw the land from Pisgah and later stood in it on the mount of transfiguration. The lesson runs against a species of prayer teaching that measures faith by refusal to accept an answer. There are matters on which God has spoken, and the faithful response is silence and obedience.

Ezekiel 45:9 turns the same word upon rulers who had made a trade of exaction. Let it suffice you is God's word to entrenched injustice: enough, remove violence and spoil, execute judgment and justice. Notice that the command to stop is joined to a command to do right. There is no repentance that consists only in ceasing; the princes must take away their exactions and then execute judgment for the people they had been fleecing.
roots_summary: Greek arkeo (G714), to be enough, to suffice; Hebrew rab (H7227), much, enough, in the phrase rab lak, let it suffice thee.
roots_lines: Greek arkeo (G714) — to be enough, be content; 1 Peter 4:3, 2 Corinthians 12:9 of grace sufficient, Hebrews 13:5.
Greek arketos (G713) — sufficient, enough; Matthew 6:34, Matthew 10:25.
Hebrew rab (H7227) — much, enough; Deuteronomy 3:26 and Ezekiel 45:9, both of God saying enough to men.
Hebrew matsa (H4672) — to find, attain, be sufficient for; Numbers 11:22 of provision for the multitude.
The two uses stand together: God is sufficient to provide, and God is the one who declares when sin has gone on long enough.
usage: “The time past of our life may suffice” — the old master has no arrears to collect.
“Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter” — a settled answer from God.
“Let it suffice you, O princes” — and then, execute judgment and justice.

pos: adj. (worthy of love; amiable; that which draws affection — rendering Greek prosphiles and Hebrew machmad)
etymology: Old English luflic, love-like. In older English it does not mean pretty; it means such as ought to be loved.
biblical_def: Lovely in the Authorized Version means worthy of love, and Paul puts it in the list of things a Christian is commanded to think about: “whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things” (Php 4:8). It stands between pure and of good report, among moral qualities, which fixes the sense: what is lovely is what deserves to be loved, not merely what pleases the eye. The word reaches its height in the bride's confession of her beloved: “His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem” (Son 5:16). David uses it of Saul and Jonathan (2Sa 1:23), refusing to let the king's ruin erase what had been honourable in him. And Ezekiel warns of a use that damns: the prophet is to his hearers “as a very lovely song of one that hath a pleasant voice… for they hear thy words, but they do them not” (Eze 33:32). A thing may be genuinely lovely and still be received wrongly — admired as performance while its command is disregarded — and that is one of the most dangerous conditions a hearer of sermons can be in.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lovely as amiable; that may excite love; possessing qualities which may invite affection; and notes that it is properly applied to what deserves love rather than to mere beauty.
webster_full: LOVELY, a. Amiable; that may excite love; possessing qualities which may invite affection.
2. Beautiful; exciting admiration; but properly, worthy to be loved.
3. In the Scriptures, applied to that which is morally excellent; as, whatsoever things are lovely.
LOVELINESS, n. Amiableness; those qualities which excite love.
scriptures: Philippians 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Song of Solomon 5:16
His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 1:23
Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions.
Ezekiel 33:32
And, lo, thou art unto them as a very lovely song of one that hath a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument: for they hear thy words, but they do them not.
corruption_summary: Loveliness is reduced to appearance, and preaching that is admired for its beauty is mistaken for preaching that has been obeyed.
corruption_paragraphs: The English word has slid from moral worth to visual charm, and the slide has consequences in the pulpit and the pew. Philippians 4:8 commands the mind to dwell on what is true, honest, just, pure, lovely — a list of moral qualities in which loveliness is the quality of deserving love. Where the word means only what is attractive, the command is heard as an instruction to think about pleasant things, and a discipline of the mind becomes a mood. What Paul enjoins is harder and better: to give the attention of the mind to things that merit it, whether or not they are comfortable.

Ezekiel 33:32 names the deadliest misuse, and it is a religious one. The people came, sat before the prophet as God's people sit, and heard the word of the LORD as a very lovely song from a man with a pleasant voice — and they did not do it. The loveliness was real; their response made it fatal. Every congregation that praises a sermon on the way out and forgets it before the week begins is under that verse. The remedy is not duller preaching but the doing of what is heard, since the beloved of Song of Solomon 5:16 who is altogether lovely is also the Lord who asks why men call Him Lord and do not the things He says.
roots_summary: Greek prosphiles (G4375), friendly toward, acceptable, lovely — Philippians 4:8 only; Hebrew machmad (H4261), a delight, object of desire; naim (H5273), pleasant.
roots_lines: Greek prosphiles (G4375) — that which calls forth love, acceptable; Philippians 4:8, its only occurrence.
Hebrew machmad (H4261) — delightful, an object of affection or desire; Song of Solomon 5:16, Lamentations 1:7.
Hebrew naim (H5273) — pleasant, sweet; 2 Samuel 1:23 of Saul and Jonathan, Psalm 133:1.
Old English luflic, love-like — the older sense is deserving of love, not merely pleasing to look at.
Philippians 4:8 places it between pure and of good report, which fixes it as a moral and not an aesthetic term.
usage: “Whatsoever things are lovely… think on these things” — a discipline of the mind, not a mood.
“He is altogether lovely” — the bride's word for her beloved.
“As a very lovely song… but they do them not” — admiration is not obedience.

pos: n. pl. (those who saw with their own eyes — rendering Greek autoptai and epoptai)
etymology: A compound of eye and witness. The Greek autoptes is literally a self-seer; epoptes is a looker-on, one admitted to behold.
biblical_def: Eyewitnesses is the New Testament's claim about its own origin. Luke opens his Gospel by grounding it in men who had seen: “Even as they delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word” (Luk 1:2). Peter, writing near the end of his life, denies the charge of invention in the plainest terms available: “For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2Pe 1:16) — and he goes on to recall the holy mount and the voice from the excellent glory. John begins his epistle with the same insistence, piling sense upon sense: “which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life” (1Jn 1:1). The apostolic office itself was constituted by this: the Lord's commission was “ye shall be witnesses unto me” (Act 1:8), and when Judas' place was filled the requirement was a man who had companied with them all the time the Lord Jesus went in and out. Christianity is therefore not a philosophy discovered by reflection but a report of events, given by men who were there, who were killed rather than withdraw it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an eye-witness as one who sees a thing done; one who has ocular view of any thing, and can therefore testify of it from his own knowledge.
webster_full: EYE-WITNESS, n. One who sees a thing done; one who has ocular view of any thing.
2. In law and in testimony, a witness who speaks of his own knowledge, and not by report of others.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; that which furnishes evidence or proof.
2. A person who knows or sees any thing; one personally present.
scriptures: Luke 1:2
Even as they delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word;
2 Peter 1:16
For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
1 John 1:1
That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life;
Acts 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
corruption_summary: The Gospels are treated as late community productions rather than the testimony of men who saw, exactly the charge Peter answered when he wrote of cunningly devised fables.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant academic account of the Gospels holds that they grew by stages within believing communities long after the events, so that what stands in them is the faith of the church rather than the report of witnesses. Peter met that account in advance and denied it by name: we have not followed cunningly devised fables… but were eyewitnesses of his majesty. Luke says the same at the head of his Gospel, naming his sources as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, and stating that he traced everything accurately in order to write it down. The apostles did not offer their conviction; they offered their eyes and ears, and they offered them under a threat that killed most of them.

John presses the point past any spiritualizing. Heard, seen with our eyes, looked upon, handled with our hands — four verbs of sense stacked in one clause about the Word of life. This is aimed at the ancient error that made Christ a phantom, and it disposes of the modern one that makes the resurrection a symbol of renewal. If the report is false the apostles were liars, not mystics; if true, it is not open to reinterpretation as inner experience. Acts 1:8 makes witness the very substance of the apostolic commission, and the church has no other foundation to stand on than the testimony of men who were there.
roots_summary: Greek autoptes (G845), a self-seer, eyewitness — Luke 1:2; epoptes (G2030), a beholder, one admitted to see — 2 Peter 1:16; martus (G3144), a witness, whence martyr.
roots_lines: Greek autoptes (G845) — one who sees for himself; Luke 1:2, its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Greek epoptes (G2030) — a looker-on, spectator; 2 Peter 1:16 only, of the apostles on the holy mount.
Greek martus (G3144) — a witness; Acts 1:8, and the word from which martyr comes, because witnesses died for the testimony.
Greek theaomai (G2300) and psēlaphaō (G5584) — to behold and to handle; the verbs of 1 John 1:1.
The apostolic requirement in Acts 1:21-22 was a man who had companied with them throughout — the office was built on sight.
usage: “Eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word” — Luke names his sources at the head of his Gospel.
“Not cunningly devised fables… but eyewitnesses of his majesty” — Peter answers the charge directly.
“Our hands have handled” — four verbs of sense in one clause.

pos: n. pl. (ancestors; those who went before in the line — rendering Greek progonoi and Hebrew abot rishonim)
etymology: From fore (before) and father. The Greek progonos means one born before; the Hebrew phrase is simply the former fathers.
biblical_def: Forefathers in Scripture is a two-edged word, and both edges are sharp. Paul can bless God for a line of godly ancestry: “I thank God, whom I serve from my forefathers with pure conscience” (2Ti 1:3) — and in the same letter he names Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, so the blessing of a covenant household is fully acknowledged. But Jeremiah uses the same word for inherited apostasy: “They are turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, which refused to hear my words; and they went after other gods to serve them” (Jer 11:10). The Psalmist prays that the coming generation “might not be as their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation; a generation that set not their heart aright, and whose spirit was not stedfast with God” (Psa 78:8). Peter is sharpest of all: the redeemed were bought “from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers” (1Pe 1:18). So Scripture will neither despise ancestry nor sanctify it. What came down from the fathers must be tested by the word of God, and what fails that test is precisely what the blood of Christ redeems a man out of — including, and especially, the religion he inherited.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines forefather as an ancestor; one who precedes another in the line of genealogy, in any degree, but usually in a remote degree.
webster_full: FOREFATHER, n. An ancestor; one who precedes another in the line of genealogy, in any degree, but usually in a remote degree.
2. In the plural, the progenitors of a family, tribe or nation, considered collectively.
TRADI'TION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity.
2. That which is handed down by tradition; and in the Scriptures often that which is vain and set against the commandment of God.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 1:3
I thank God, whom I serve from my forefathers with pure conscience, that without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day;
Jeremiah 11:10

They are turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, which refused to hear my words; and they went after other gods to serve them: the house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant which I made with their fathers.
1 Peter 1:18
Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers;
Psalm 78:8
