And might not be as their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation; a generation that set not their heart aright, and whose spirit was not stedfast with God.
corruption_summary: Inheritance is made the standard, so that what the fathers did is treated as proof that it is right — or, at the other extreme, every inherited thing is discarded because it is inherited.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome builds a doctrine of tradition on the fathers, setting an unwritten deposit beside the Scriptures as a second authority. First Peter 1:18 stands squarely against it: what came by tradition from the fathers was the very vain conversation from which the blood of Christ redeemed them. Scripture honours faithful ancestry — Paul serves God from his forefathers, Timothy has an unfeigned faith that dwelt first in his grandmother — but the honour is given because their faith was true, not because it was old. Antiquity is not a warrant. Jeremiah's generation had the longest religious pedigree in the world and had inherited the iniquities with it.

The opposite error is now the more fashionable: to treat inheritance itself as a defect, and every practice received from the fathers as a limitation to be outgrown. Psalm 78 refutes this by its own structure. The Psalmist tells the coming generation the works of God precisely so that they might not be as their fathers, stubborn and rebellious — the remedy for a bad inheritance is a better one, faithfully handed on, not the abolition of handing on. A church that keeps nothing from its fathers has not escaped tradition; it has merely exchanged an old one for whatever the present decade supplies.
roots_summary: Greek progonos (G4269), an ancestor, forefather — 2 Timothy 1:3, 1 Timothy 5:4; Hebrew ab (H1), father, with rishon (H7223), former, first.
roots_lines: Greek progonos (G4269) — one born before, an ancestor; 2 Timothy 1:3 and 1 Timothy 5:4, of duty to parents.
Hebrew ab (H1) — father, in the immediate and the remote sense; the ordinary word for ancestor.
Hebrew rishon (H7223) — former, first, ancestral; joined with ab in Jeremiah 11:10.
Greek patroparadotos (G3970) — handed down from the fathers; 1 Peter 1:18, where what was handed down was vain.
Scripture praises and indicts ancestry with the same word, and the test in both cases is the word of God.
usage: “Whom I serve from my forefathers with pure conscience” — godly ancestry gratefully owned.
“Turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers” — the other inheritance.
“Redeemed… from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers” — the blood buys men out of inherited religion.

pos: n. (departure out of life; death — rendering Greek exodos)
etymology: Latin decessus, a going away, from decedere, to depart. The Greek behind both New Testament uses is exodos — the same word as the second book of Moses.
biblical_def: Decease occurs twice in the New Testament, and in both places the Greek is exodos, an exodus. On the mount of transfiguration Moses and Elijah “appeared in glory, and spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luk 9:31). Every word is weighted. The subject of the conversation in glory was the death of Christ; the term for it was exodus, so that the cross is set forth as the true going-out of which the deliverance from Egypt was the shadow; and it was something He would accomplish, a work brought to completion, not a fate suffered. Peter uses the same word of his own death: “Moreover I will endeavour that ye may be able after my decease to have these things always in remembrance” (2Pe 1:15) — and his concern is not for himself but that the church should have the truth in permanent form when he is gone. Behind both stands the appointment: “it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27), and Paul's calm reckoning of his own end: “the time of my departure is at hand” (2Ti 4:6). For the believer death is called a going out, because he is going somewhere; the word itself is an argument against annihilation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines decease as literally a departure; hence, death; departure from this life; and notes it is used of the death of human beings only.
webster_full: DECE'ASE, n. Literally, departure; hence, death; departure from this life; applied to human beings only.
DECE'ASE, v.i. To depart from this life; to die.
EX'ODUS, n. Departure from a place; particularly, the departure of the Israelites from Egypt, and the book which records it.
DEPART'URE, n. A going away; removal from the present life; death.
scriptures: Luke 9:31
Who appeared in glory, and spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem.
2 Peter 1:15
Moreover I will endeavour that ye may be able after my decease to have these things always in remembrance.
Hebrews 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
2 Timothy 4:6
For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand.
corruption_summary: Death is made a natural passage or an extinction, and the appointment with judgment that Scripture attaches to it is quietly removed.
corruption_paragraphs: Two false comforts are offered at every graveside. The first says death is a natural part of life, a return to the cycle of things, and therefore nothing to fear. Scripture calls death the last enemy and the wages of sin, and Hebrews attaches to it the clause that no natural account can absorb: after this the judgment. The second says death is simple extinction, and so the account is closed by non-existence. The very word Luke chose forbids it. An exodus is a going out to somewhere; Israel did not cease at the Red Sea, she crossed it.

Luke 9:31 also forbids a third error — the reading of the cross as tragedy or miscarriage. Moses and Elijah spoke of a decease Christ would accomplish at Jerusalem, a work to be finished, and it was finished. Peter's use in his own case shows the settled mind this produces in a servant of God facing execution: his last recorded anxiety is not about dying but about whether the church will have these things in remembrance after he is gone. That is what death looks like to a man who knows it as an exodus.
roots_summary: Greek exodos (G1841), an exit, a going out, hence death — Luke 9:31, 2 Peter 1:15, and Hebrews 11:22 of the departing of Israel; analusis (G359), a loosing, departure.
roots_lines: Greek exodos (G1841) — an exit or departure; Luke 9:31 of Christ's death, 2 Peter 1:15 of Peter's, Hebrews 11:22 of Israel leaving Egypt.
Greek analusis (G359) — a loosing, as of a ship from moorings; 2 Timothy 4:6, the companion image.
Greek teleutao (G5053) — to finish life, decease; Matthew 2:19, Acts 7:15.
The choice of exodus makes the cross the true deliverance of which Egypt was the type.
Christ did not merely undergo His decease; Luke says He would accomplish it — a work completed, not a fate endured.
usage: “Spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem” — an exodus, and a finished work.
“After my decease… these things always in remembrance” — Peter's last care was for the church.
“Appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” — the clause no natural account can absorb.

pos: n. (a going away; a loosing from moorings; death — rendering Greek analusis)
etymology: Latin departire, to divide, part from. The Greek analusis is a nautical and military word: the loosing of a ship's cables, or the striking of a camp.
biblical_def: Departure is Paul's word for his own death, written in prison with the sword in view: “For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand” (2Ti 4:6). The Greek is analusis, the loosing of a ship from its moorings or the taking down of a tent to march. Neither image contains any thought of ending; both are words of setting out. The same apostle had written earlier from another prison, “I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better” (Php 1:23), which defines the destination and settles the question of the intermediate state: to depart is to be with Christ, immediately and consciously. And he draws the account of his life in the next breath after announcing his departure: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7). The word has a second, ordinary use of grief at any parting, as when Tyre falls and the isles are troubled at her departure (Eze 26:18). But for the believer the ship is not sinking; it is sailing, and the moorings that hold it here are cut by the same hand that appointed the voyage.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines departure as the act of going away; a removal; a desisting or deviating from; and, applied to human life, death, decease, removal from the present state of existence.
webster_full: DEPART'URE, n. The act of going away; a moving from or leaving a place.
2. Death; decease; removal from the present life.
3. A forsaking; abandonment; as, a departure from evil, or from the faith.
4. In navigation, the distance a ship has made east or west from the meridian of the place she left.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 4:6
For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand.
Philippians 1:23
For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:
2 Timothy 4:7
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Ezekiel 26:18
Now shall the isles tremble in the day of thy fall; yea, the isles that are in the sea shall be troubled at thy departure.
corruption_summary: The believer's death is treated either as unconscious sleep until the resurrection or as an immediate perfection that makes the resurrection of the body unnecessary.
corruption_paragraphs: Philippians 1:23 settles the first question in six words: to depart, and to be with Christ. Paul is not weighing continued labour against unconsciousness; he is weighing it against a presence he calls far better, and no man prefers oblivion to fruitful ministry. The doctrine of soul sleep cannot survive the comparison Paul actually makes. The believer who dies is with Christ that day — as the Lord told the thief — consciously, in the intermediate state, awaiting the redemption of the body.

The opposite error takes the comfort of that verse and stops there, as though the soul's presence with Christ were the whole hope and the body an outgrown garment. That is Greek, not Christian. Paul who longed to depart also called death the last enemy and set the whole weight of hope on the resurrection of the body at the last trump. Departure is the loosing of a ship for a voyage that has a landfall: to be with Christ, then to be raised. Both must be preached, or the church will comfort its mourners with half a hope.
roots_summary: Greek analusis (G359), a loosing, departure — 2 Timothy 4:6 only; the verb analuo (G360), to loose or return, in Philippians 1:23 and Luke 12:36.
roots_lines: Greek analusis (G359) — a loosing of moorings or striking of a tent; 2 Timothy 4:6, its only occurrence.
Greek analuo (G360) — to unloose, depart; Philippians 1:23 of departing to be with Christ, Luke 12:36 of the lord returning from the wedding.
Greek exodos (G1841) — the companion word, a going out; Luke 9:31 and 2 Peter 1:15.
Hebrew yatsa (H3318) — to go out, depart; the common Old Testament verb behind departures of every kind.
The image is not of a light going out but of a ship untied — departure implies a destination.
usage: “The time of my departure is at hand” — the moorings are being cut, not the light put out.
“To depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better” — the destination named.
“I have finished my course” — the account drawn in the same breath.

pos: n. pl. (the successive stages of a march; travels — rendering Hebrew massa and Greek hodoiporia)
etymology: From journey, Old French journee, a day's travel. The Hebrew massa means literally a pulling up of tent stakes — a departure by stages.
biblical_def: Journeyings is the Authorized Version's word for a life or a nation lived in stages. Of Israel: “Thus were the journeyings of the children of Israel according to their armies, when they set forward” (Num 10:28), and Moses was commanded to write them down: “And Moses wrote their goings out according to their journeys by the commandment of the LORD” (Num 33:2). The Hebrew word means the pulling up of tent pegs. A journeying is not a distance covered but a camp struck — the settled place abandoned at the command of God because the cloud moved. Paul uses the Greek equivalent in his catalogue of sufferings: “In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren” (2Co 11:26). The apostolic ministry was itinerant and dangerous, and the perils are listed by terrain and by company — including, last and worst, false brethren. Hebrews gathers the whole doctrine: the patriarchs “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13), which is the settled self-understanding of the people of God. They died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines journey as travel by land; a passage from one place to another; and journeyings as the successive stages or removals of a people on the march.
webster_full: JOUR'NEY, n. The travel of a day; hence, travel by land to any distance and for any time.
2. Passage from one place to another; as, a long journey.
JOUR'NEYING, ppr. Traveling; passing from place to place.
JOUR'NEYINGS, n. plural. The successive removals or stages of a people on the march, as those of Israel in the wilderness.
scriptures: Numbers 10:28
Thus were the journeyings of the children of Israel according to their armies, when they set forward.
2 Corinthians 11:26

In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren;
Hebrews 11:13

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Numbers 33:2
And Moses wrote their goings out according to their journeys by the commandment of the LORD: and these are their journeys according to their goings out.
corruption_summary: The pilgrim character of the Christian life is exchanged for permanence here, and the word journey is annexed to a private spirituality with no destination and no command.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 33 is a chapter of stage-names, written down at God's command, and it exists to teach a settled people that they were once a marching one. Hebrews 11:13 says the patriarchs confessed themselves strangers and pilgrims on the earth — a confession, publicly made, not a mood. Where the church forgets it, the marks are obvious: possessions held tightly, roots put down as though the camp were the country, and a Christianity indistinguishable in its ambitions from the world it passes through. The tent pegs come up at the command of God, and a man who has driven his in too deep will resent the cloud when it moves.

The modern religious use of journey runs the opposite way and empties the word from the other end. A journey with no destination, no map and no commander is not a pilgrimage but a wandering, and Scripture has a word for that too — the forty years were a judgment, not a spirituality. Israel's journeyings were by the commandment of the LORD, recorded stage by stage, toward a land already promised. Paul's were toward cities where Christ was not named. Both had a road and an end. Nothing in the Christian life is a journey merely for the travelling.
roots_summary: Hebrew massa (H4550), a pulling up of stakes, a setting forward by stages — Numbers 10:28, 33:2; Greek hodoiporia (G3597), a journeying, travel — 2 Corinthians 11:26, John 4:6.
roots_lines: Hebrew massa (H4550) — a departure by striking the tents; Numbers 10:28 and throughout Numbers 33.
Hebrew nasa (H5265) — to pull up stakes, journey; the verb behind the noun, used of every stage of the wilderness march.
Greek hodoiporia (G3597) — a journeying, travel; 2 Corinthians 11:26 and John 4:6 of the Lord wearied with His journey.
Greek parepidemos (G3927) — a sojourner, pilgrim; Hebrews 11:13, 1 Peter 1:1 and 2:11.
The Hebrew image is the tent peg: a journeying begins with leaving a place one had made comfortable.
usage: “Moses wrote their goings out… by the commandment of the LORD” — the stages were recorded on purpose.
“In journeyings often… in perils among false brethren” — the last peril is the worst.
“Strangers and pilgrims on the earth” — a confession, not a mood.

pos: v.t. (to untie, set free — rendering Greek luo, used of the latchet of a sandal)
etymology: From un- and loose, an intensive rather than a reversal. The Greek luo means simply to loosen; the office in view was the lowest household task, untying a master's sandal.
biblical_def: Unloose appears in the New Testament in one setting only: John the Baptist measuring himself against Christ. “There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose” (Mar 1:7); “one mightier than I cometh, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire” (Luk 3:16); “whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose” (Joh 1:27). To untie a man's sandal was work so low that a Hebrew slave could not be required to do it; it was left to Gentile servants and to children. John, whom the Lord called the greatest born of women, says he is not fit for that office toward Christ. The comparison is not modesty but measurement: John baptizes with water, the One coming baptizes with the Holy Ghost and with fire. And John draws the only conclusion a true minister can draw: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (Joh 3:30). Mark adds stoop down, so the picture is complete — the greatest of the prophets, bending to the dust at another man's feet, and saying he is not worthy of the position.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unloose as to loose; to untie; to set free from bonds or fastening; and notes that the prefix does not reverse but intensifies the sense of loosing.
webster_full: UNLOO'SE, v.t. To loose; to untie; to unbind; to free from fastening.
UNLOO'SE, v.i. To fall in pieces; to lose all connection or union.
LATCH'ET, n. The string that fastens a shoe or sandal.
LOOSE, v.t. To untie or unbind; to free from any fastening; to release from restraint.
scriptures: Mark 1:7
And preached, saying, There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose.
Luke 3:16

John answered, saying unto them all, I indeed baptize you with water; but one mightier than I cometh, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire:
John 1:27
He it is, who coming after me is preferred before me, whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose.
John 3:30
He must increase, but I must decrease.
corruption_summary: The minister is exalted into the place of the Master, and John's measurement of himself is treated as excessive humility rather than plain accuracy.
corruption_paragraphs: The whole ministerial disease of the age is answered by a sandal strap. John the Baptist drew crowds out of every city, baptized the multitudes, and was reckoned by the Lord Himself as the greatest born of women — and he said he was not worthy to perform the lowest household service for the One coming after him. This is not self-abasement for effect; it is an accurate reading of the distance between a herald and his King. Wherever a preacher's name, brand, or personality becomes the thing gathered around, that distance has been forgotten, and John's sentence stands as the correction.

Luke gives the ground of the comparison, and it is doctrinal rather than temperamental: I indeed baptize you with water; but… he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire. The minister administers a sign; Christ does the thing signified. No man can give the Spirit, regenerate a heart, or forgive a sin, and the office is honourable precisely because it points past itself. John 3:30 is therefore not a saying for particularly humble ministers but the rule of the office: He must increase, but I must decrease. A ministry not decreasing is in the wrong direction.
roots_summary: Greek luo (G3089), to loosen, untie — of the sandal latchet in Mark 1:7, Luke 3:16, John 1:27; himas (G2438), the thong or latchet itself.
roots_lines: Greek luo (G3089) — to loose, untie, dissolve; over forty times, including the loosing of Lazarus and of Satan.
Greek himas (G2438) — a strap or thong; the latchet of the sandal in all three Gospel sayings, and the scourging thongs of Acts 22:25.
Greek bastazo (G941) — to bear or carry; Matthew 3:11 has John unworthy to bear the shoes, the same office in another form.
Untying a sandal was the task of the lowest servant in a house, and Jewish teaching excused a Hebrew bondman from it.
Mark alone adds stoop down, completing the picture of the greatest prophet bending to the dust.
usage: “Not worthy to stoop down and unloose” — the lowest service in the house, and John says he is unfit for it.
“I indeed baptize you with water… he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost” — sign and substance.
“He must increase, but I must decrease” — the rule of every true ministry.
